q: "Double coincidence of wants" is an essential feature of which system?
o: Modern banking system
Barter system
Digital UPI system
Cheque system
e: In a barter system where goods are directly exchanged without money, double coincidence of wants is an essential feature.

q: How does money eliminate the need for double coincidence of wants?
o: By acting as an intermediate step or medium of exchange
By stopping production of goods
By doubling all prices
By banning domestic markets
e: Since money acts as an intermediate in the exchange process, it is called a medium of exchange and eliminates double coincidence of wants.

q: Who issues currency notes on behalf of the Central Government in India?
o: State Bank of India (SBI)
Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
Finance Commission
Commercial banks
e: In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issues currency notes on behalf of the Central Government.

q: Why is modern currency accepted as a medium of exchange even though paper notes and coins have no use of their own?
o: Because the currency is authorised by the government of the country
Because it is made of pure gold and silver
Because it can be consumed like grain
Because foreign banks enforce it
e: Unlike earlier commodities or precious metals, modern currency is without any use of its own, yet accepted because it is authorised by the government.

q: In India, settlement in which currency cannot be legally refused by any person or organisation?
o: US Dollar
Rupee
British Pound
Gold coins
e: No individual in India can legally refuse a payment made in Rupees, making the rupee widely accepted as a medium of exchange.

q: Deposits in bank accounts that can be withdrawn on demand are called—
o: Fixed deposits only
Demand Deposits
Informal deposits
Cash reserve
e: Since deposits in bank accounts can be withdrawn on demand, these deposits are called demand deposits and serve as a key modern form of money.

q: What is a "Cheque"?
o: A loan sanction letter from RBI
A paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from the person’s account to the person in whose name the cheque has been issued
A foreign currency note
A land mortgage deed
e: A cheque is a paper instructing the bank to pay a specific amount from one’s account to the named recipient, settling payments without cash.

q: Banks in India hold roughly what percentage of their deposits as cash with themselves on any given day?
o: About 2%
About 15%
About 50%
About 85%
e: Banks in India hold about 15% of their deposits as cash as provision to pay depositors who might come to withdraw money on any given day.

q: What is the main source of income for commercial banks?
o: Account opening fees charged to depositors
The difference between the interest charged from borrowers and what is paid to depositors
Profits from printing currency notes
Tax collection commission
e: Banks charge a higher interest rate on loans than what they offer on deposits; this difference is their main source of income.

q: What is "Collateral" in the context of credit?
o: A discount on the interest rate
An asset that the borrower owns (land, building, vehicle, livestock, deposits with banks) and uses as a guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid
A ration card only
A loan waiver certificate
e: Collateral is an asset owned by the borrower pledged as a guarantee to the lender until the loan is repaid.

q: What collectively constitutes the "Terms of Credit"?
o: Interest rate, collateral, documentation requirement, and the mode of repayment
Only the borrower’s age and address
Only the currency denomination
Bank branch opening hours
e: Interest rate, collateral, documentation requirement, and mode of repayment together comprise the Terms of Credit.

q: When credit pushes a borrower into a situation from which recovery is very painful and repayment requires taking fresh loans or selling land, it is called—
o: Demand deposit
Debt trap
Inflation
Liberalisation
e: As illustrated by Swapna’s groundnut crop failure, credit can push the borrower into a Debt Trap from which recovery is very painful.

q: Which of the following is a source of "Formal Sector Loans"?
o: Moneylenders
Traders
Banks and Cooperatives
Friends and relatives
e: Banks and cooperatives are formal sector credit sources, whereas moneylenders, traders, employers, and relatives/friends are informal sources.

q: Who supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans in India?
o: Gram Panchayat
Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
World Trade Organisation
Moneylenders Association
e: The Reserve Bank of India supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans; no organisation supervises informal lenders.

q: Which of the following are sources of "Informal Sector Credit"?
o: Moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives, and friends
State Bank of India and NABARD
Krishak Cooperative and Regional Rural Banks
Public sector banks only
e: Informal lenders include moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives, and friends.

q: A typical Self-Help Group (SHG) in rural India has how many members from one neighbourhood?
o: 2–4 members
15–20 members
100–150 members
More than 500 members
e: A typical SHG has 15–20 members, usually belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly.

q: Who founded the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh as a small project in the 1970s (later awarded the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize)?
o: Prof. Muhammad Yunus
Amartya Sen
Jawaharlal Nehru
Raghuram Rajan
e: Prof. Muhammad Yunus started Grameen Bank of Bangladesh in the 1970s and received the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize.

q: Almost all of the borrowers of the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh belong to which group?
o: Large urban industrialists
Women belonging to poorest sections of society
Senior civil servants
Foreign corporations
e: Almost all borrowers of Grameen Bank are women from the poorest sections of society, proving poor women are reliable borrowers.

q: Which major barrier that prevents poor households from getting bank loans do Self-Help Groups (SHGs) help overcome?
o: Lack of collateral
Lack of currency notes
Zero interest rates
Lack of local roads
e: SHGs help borrowers overcome the problem of lack of collateral because banks lend directly to the group after one or two years of regular savings.

q: Before the introduction of coins, what objects were commonly used as money by Indians?
o: Paper cheques
Grains and cattle
Plastic debit cards
Steel rods
e: Before the introduction of coins, a variety of objects were used as money—since the very early ages, Indians used grains and cattle as money.

q: After metallic coins (gold, silver, copper), which modern forms of currency came into circulation?
o: Paper notes and modern coins (alongside bank deposits and cheques)
Rough stone blocks
Only cowrie shells
Salt blocks
e: Modern forms of money include currency (paper notes and coins) and demand deposits with banks.

q: What does "Credit" (loan) refer to?
o: An agreement in which the lender supplies the borrower with money, goods, or services in return for the promise of future payment
Free charity with no repayment obligation
Cash salary paid by employers
Government tax collection
e: Credit refers to an agreement in which the lender supplies money, goods, or services to the borrower in return for the promise of future repayment.

q: After a year or two of regular savings, what is a Self-Help Group (SHG) eligible to receive?
o: Foreign passports
Loan from a bank in the name of the group
Free agricultural land
Tax exemption forever
e: If the SHG is regular in savings, after a year or two it becomes eligible for availing of loan from the bank, sanctioned in the name of the group.

q: According to the NCERT graph on credit sources in urban India, roughly what percentage of loans taken by rich households come from formal sources?
o: Only 15%
About 90%
Over 100%
e: NCERT’s urban credit graph shows 90% of loans of rich households come from formal sources (only 10% informal), whereas 85% of poor households’ loans come from informal sources.

q: In the NCERT chart for urban households, roughly what percentage of loans taken by poor households come from informal sources?
e: 85% of the loans taken by poor households in urban areas are from informal sources (only 15% formal).

q: In NCERT’s Sonpur credit examples, the "Krishak Cooperative" near Sonpur has roughly how many farmer members?
o: 150 farmers
2,300 farmers
50,000 farmers
Only 20 farmers
e: Krishak Cooperative near Sonpur has 2,300 farmers as members who pool deposits as collateral to obtain a large bank loan for members.

q: Why are demand deposits considered a form of money in the modern economy?
o: Because the facility of cheques against demand deposits makes it possible to directly settle payments without cash, and money can be withdrawn anytime
Because banks permanently lock deposits for 50 years
Because banks charge 50% penalty on withdrawals
Because only RBI holds demand deposits
e: Demand deposits share the essential features of money because cheques against them settle payments directly without cash.

q: Megha took a Rs 5 lakh housing loan from a bank at 12% interest over 10 years, submitting employment/salary records and keeping the new house documents with the bank until full repayment. What do the new house papers serve as?
o: Demand deposit
Collateral
Cheque
Unemployment allowance
e: The papers of the new house retained by the bank until the loan with interest is repaid act as Collateral.

q: In Sonpur village, whom does Rama, a landless agricultural labourer, mainly depend upon for credit?
o: Commercial banks
Her employer, a medium landowner in Sonpur
Krishak Cooperative
World Bank
e: Lacking collateral, Rama depends on her employer-landowner for credit at 5% per month interest and repays by working for the landowner.

q: Besides loans and savings, what social issues do SHG meetings provide a platform for rural women to discuss and act upon?
o: Health, nutrition, domestic violence, and other social issues
Only international stock futures
Only cricket rules
Space satellite launches
e: SHGs not only make women financially self-reliant, their regular meetings also provide a platform to discuss and act on social issues like health, nutrition, and domestic violence.

q: A shoe manufacturer wants to buy wheat in a barter economy without money. What specific difficulty does he face?
o: He must find a wheat-growing farmer who not only wants to sell wheat, but simultaneously wants to buy shoes in exchange
He must fill out a bank cheque
He must get permission from RBI
Farmers will demand gold bullion
e: Both parties must agree to sell and buy each other’s commodities simultaneously—known as double coincidence of wants.

q: Banks keep only about 15% of their deposits as cash and lend out the rest. Why does this system work smoothly on any typical day?
o: Because on any particular day only some of its many depositors come to withdraw cash, so the bank can easily manage with about 15% cash
Because people are forbidden from withdrawing money
Because banks refuse all withdrawals
Because cheques replace all bank accounts
e: Since on any particular day only some depositors come to withdraw cash, banks comfortably meet demand with ~15% reserve while lending out the major share.

q: How do banks act as mediators in the economy?
o: They mediate between those who have surplus funds (depositors) and those who are in need of these funds (borrowers)
They only collect property taxes
They directly manufacture industrial tools
They issue passports to citizens
e: Banks mediate between depositors with surplus funds and borrowers needing funds for economic activities.

q: Why did credit play a positive role for Salim (shoe manufacturer) yet push Swapna (groundnut farmer) into a debt trap?
o: Salim met working capital needs, completed production on time, earned profit and repaid credit; Swapna’s crop failed despite pesticides, leaving her unable to repay and forcing fresh borrowing
Salim defaulted on every payment
Swapna produced leather shoes
Salim received zero-repayment charity
e: Whether credit is useful depends on the risks in the situation and whether there is support in case of loss; Salim succeeded while Swapna’s crop failure triggered a debt trap.

q: From which TWO sources did Salim obtain credit to meet his working capital needs for the 3,000-pair order?
o: (1) Leather supplier on promise to pay later, and (2) cash loan/advance payment for 1,000 pairs from the large trader with a promise to deliver by month-end
(1) World Bank and (2) IMF
(1) SHGs and (2) MGNREGA
(1) Selling his workshop and (2) borrowing from RBI
e: Salim obtained credit from two sources: leather on credit from the supplier, and cash advance for 1,000 pairs from the large trader.

q: Why do lenders ask for "Collateral" while lending money?
o: If the borrower fails to repay the loan, the lender has the right to sell the asset or collateral to obtain payment
To seize borrower assets even when loans are repaid
To ensure 0% interest on all loans
Merely to increase paperwork
e: Collateral acts as security for the lender; upon default, the lender has the legal right to sell the collateral asset to recover the loan.

q: Compare the credit terms accessed by Arun (7 acres land) and Shyamal (1.5 acres) in Sonpur village:
o: Arun got a bank loan at 8.5% per annum repayable over 3 years and could store potatoes in cold storage, whereas Shyamal had to borrow from an agricultural trader at 36% per annum (3% per month) promising to sell his crop to him
Shyamal got 2% bank credit while Arun paid 60%
Both received interest-free grants
Arun failed to get any bank credit
e: Arun received low-interest bank credit (8.5% p.a.) allowing crop storage for better prices, whereas small farmer Shyamal paid 36% p.a. to a trader with forced crop-sale terms.

q: How does the Krishak Cooperative near Sonpur enable farmers to get cheap bank credit?
o: It accepts deposits from its 2,300 members and uses those pooled deposits as collateral to obtain a large bank loan, which is then lent to members
It sells members’ farms every season
It borrows from moneylenders at 60% interest
It prints its own notes
e: Members’ pooled deposits serve as collateral for a large bank loan, enabling the cooperative to lend cheaply for cultivation, implements, trade, fisheries, and housing.

q: In what ways does the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) supervise the functioning of banks?
o: RBI monitors that banks actually maintain the minimum cash balance and sees that banks lend not just to profit-making businesses/traders, but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries, and small borrowers
RBI only prints coins
RBI forbids banks from lending to farmers
RBI audits village moneylenders daily
e: Banks periodically submit information to RBI on how much they are lending, to whom, and at what interest rate.

q: Why is borrowing from informal sector lenders often harmful for poor borrowers?
o: No organisation supervises them; they charge much higher interest rates, use unfair means to recover money, leaving borrowers with less income or trapped in debt
They charge lower rates than banks
They give 30-year interest-free terms
They are strictly audited by RBI
e: Higher cost of borrowing means a large part of borrower earnings goes to repay the loan, leaving less income and risking a debt trap.

q: Why is "cheap and affordable credit" crucial for a country’s development?
o: It allows more people to borrow cheaply for growing crops, doing business, setting up small-scale industries, or trading in goods, raising incomes and output
It forces all banks to close down
It bans small workshops
It reduces agricultural output
e: Cheap and affordable formal credit empowers people to borrow safely for farming, business, and small-scale industries without high interest costs crushing their income.

q: Why do poor households in India still depend heavily on informal sources of credit rather than banks?
o: Banks are not present everywhere in rural India, and bank loans require proper documents and collateral which poor people usually lack
Police bar poor villagers from banks
Moneylenders charge lower interest than banks
Banks refuse Indian currency deposits
e: Absence of collateral and documentation bars the poor from bank loans, whereas informal lenders like moneylenders know borrowers personally and lend without collateral.

q: Why are banks willing to lend to poor women organised in Self-Help Groups (SHGs) even without traditional collateral?
o: Because any case of non-repayment of loan by any one member is followed up seriously by other members in the group, ensuring high repayment discipline
Because banks never expect repayment
Because SHG members pledge gold palaces
Because SHGs charge 100% interest
e: Peer monitoring and collective group responsibility ensure serious follow-up on repayments, making SHGs highly reliable borrowers for banks.

q: How do members of an SHG initially use their own pooled savings before getting a bank loan?
o: Members can take small loans from the group itself at a low interest rate (much lower than what moneylenders charge) to meet their needs
All savings belong exclusively to the group secretary
Savings are locked away without lending
Interest rates inside SHGs exceed 80%
e: Members pool small regular savings (Rs 25–100+) and can borrow small loans from the group itself at an interest rate much lower than moneylenders charge.

q: In NCERT’s example, shoe manufacturer M. Salim pays leather supplier Prem Kumar Rs 20,000 by issuing a cheque. What actually happens in the banks?
o: Rs 20,000 is transferred directly from M. Salim’s bank account to Prem Kumar’s bank account without any cash payment
Both bank accounts are frozen
RBI prints new Rs 20,000 notes
Prem Kumar pays a 20% cheque tax
e: The money is transferred from one bank account to another in a couple of days, completing the transaction without any cash payment.

q: From whom did Swapna (a small farmer) borrow money to cultivate groundnuts, and what did she eventually have to do to repay the growing debt?
o: From a cooperative at 0% interest
From a moneylender; when pests ruined her crop and debt grew, she had to sell a part of her land to pay off the debt
From World Bank on a 20-year grant
From a commercial bank and doubled her farm area
e: After pests hit her crop, Swapna could not repay the moneylender; debt spiralled so much that even after a normal crop next year she had to sell a part of her land.

q: After grains and cattle, which metallic coins were used in India for centuries before modern paper currency?
o: Only iron and aluminium coins
Only plastic tokens
Gold, silver, and copper coins
Only zinc bars
e: Following grains and cattle came the use of metallic coins—gold, silver, copper coins—a phase which continued well into the last century.

q: In Megha’s Rs 5 lakh housing loan example in NCERT, what were the interest rate, repayment duration, and mode of repayment?
o: 24% per annum over 2 years
12% per annum, to be repaid in 10 years in monthly instalments
36% per annum paid in crops
0% interest payable after 50 years
e: Megha took a Rs 5 lakh loan at an annual interest rate of 12%, repayable over 10 years in monthly instalments.

q: For which purposes does the Krishak Cooperative provide loans to its farmer members?
o: Only foreign leisure travel
Only stock market speculation
Purchasing agricultural implements, cultivation and agricultural trade, fishery loans, construction of houses, and various other expenses
Building luxury shopping malls
e: Krishak Cooperative provides loans for purchasing agricultural implements, cultivation, agricultural trade, fisheries, house construction, and other expenses.

q: At what monthly interest rate does Rama (landless agricultural labourer in Sonpur) borrow from her employer-landowner?
o: 0.5% per month
1% per month
2% per month
5% per month (i.e. 60% per annum)
e: Rama borrows from her landowner-employer at an interest rate of 5% per month and repays it by working for the landowner.

q: Why do people generally deposit their surplus cash with banks?
o: Because banks charge extra fees for safety
Because money is safe with banks, earns interest, and depositors can withdraw it whenever they require
Because notes expire in 7 days at home
Because home safes are banned by law
e: People deposit surplus money in banks because it stays safe, earns an interest amount, and can be withdrawn anytime on demand.

q: How does the cheque facility settle transactions without the use of physical cash?
o: Gold coins are couriered instead of rupees
A cheque instructs the bank to transfer funds directly from the payer’s account to the payee’s account
Cheques convert into grain
Cheques work only across foreign borders
e: Cheques directly settle payments between one bank account and another without physical currency changing hands.

q: Why are formal bank loan terms easier for a salaried employee or large farmer than for a landless casual worker?
o: Because salaried employees and big farmers possess income documentation and collateral assets required by banks, which landless workers lack
Because banks dislike rural residents
Because landless citizens are banned from entering banks
Because salaried borrowers pay 50% interest
e: Formal banks demand proper documents and collateral; lacking assets and formal pay slips keeps poor borrowers out of bank loans.

q: What information must commercial banks periodically submit to the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)?
o: Only branch electricity bills
Details on how much they are lending, to whom they are lending (including small cultivators/borrowers), and at what interest rate
Staff vacation preferences
Village moneylenders’ home addresses
e: Periodically, banks have to submit information to the RBI on how much they are lending, to whom, at what interest rate, etc.

q: Which feature accurately distinguishes informal credit lenders from formal lenders?
o: They are supervised by RBI at 4% interest
There is no supervising organisation, interest rates are much higher, and unfair means may be used to get money back
They lend strictly to civil servants
They prohibit repayment before 10 years
e: With no supervising body, informal lenders charge high interest rates and can use unfair recovery methods.

q: What is the typical regular saving per member and group size of a rural Self-Help Group (SHG) mentioned in NCERT?
o: 500 members saving Rs 50,000 daily
15–20 members pooling Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more regularly depending on ability to save
2 members saving Rs 5 annually
100 members donating gold ornaments
e: A typical SHG has 15–20 members from one neighbourhood saving from Rs 25 to Rs 100 or more regularly depending on their saving capacity.

q: What self-employment purposes does an SHG bank loan typically support for its members?
o: Releasing mortgaged land, buying working capital (seeds, fertilisers, bamboo, cloth), housing materials, and acquiring assets like sewing machines, handlooms, or cattle
Purchasing international flight tickets
Speculating in stock exchanges
Paying bribes to officials
e: SHG loans help members release mortgaged land, meet working capital needs for seeds/inputs/raw materials, and buy income-earning assets like sewing machines, handlooms, or cattle.

q: Which two formal institutions need to expand their lending especially in rural areas to ensure cheap and affordable credit?
o: Moneylenders and crop traders
Employers and private landlords
Banks and Cooperative Societies
Foreign currency brokers only
e: It is necessary that banks and cooperatives increase their lending particularly in the rural areas so that dependence on informal credit reduces.

q: According to NCERT’s graph of urban households’ credit sources, how do well-off vs poor households compare?
o: Households with few assets take 53% informal (47% formal) and poor households take 85% informal, whereas rich households take 90% formal (only 10% informal)
Poor households get 90% formal bank loans
Rich households borrow 85% from moneylenders
All income groups share an identical 50-50 split
e: NCERT Graph 2 shows poor households borrow 85% informally (only 15% formally), households with few assets 53% informally, well-off 72% formally, and rich households 90% formally.

q: Why are Self-Help Groups considered building blocks of the organisation of the rural poor?
o: Because they lend exclusively to wealthy landlords
Because they organise rural women, overcome collateral barriers, build financial self-reliance, and offer regular forums to act on health, nutrition, and domestic violence
Because they replace parliamentary elections
Because they shut down rural cooperatives
e: SHGs act as building blocks for organising the rural poor—delivering collateral-free timely credit, self-reliance for women, and collective forums for social welfare.

q: What would happen if ALL depositors suddenly showed up on the same day demanding all their cash from a bank, and what principle does this reveal?
o: The bank would be unable to pay everyone immediately because it holds only ~15% in cash and lends out the major portion to borrowers
The bank prints unlimited currency notes on site
The bank keeps 100% of deposits idle in vaults
Borrowers immediately lose their loans
e: Modern fractional-reserve banking relies on the fact that only some depositors withdraw on any single day, enabling banks to channel ~85% of funds into productive loans.

q: Rich households get 90% of their credit from cheap formal sources while poor households rely 85% on expensive informal lenders. What are the economic consequences?
o: Rich households borrow cheaply to expand assets and income, whereas poor borrowers lose much of their earnings to exorbitant informal interest, widening inequality
Poor households get rich faster due to moneylenders
Informal interest is zero across villages
Economic disparities vanish quickly
e: Unequal access to cheap formal credit leaves poor borrowers paying high interest that consumes their income; hence formal credit must expand especially to poorer households.

q: Which TWO steps best address the problem of unequal access to formal sector credit in India?
o: (1) Expanding formal bank and cooperative branches/lending in rural areas, and (2) linking poor households to collateral-free bank credit through Self-Help Groups (SHGs)
(1) Closing rural bank branches, and (2) encouraging moneylenders
(1) Raising bank collateral requirements tenfold, and (2) banning cooperatives
(1) Ending RBI supervision, and (2) halting rural loans
e: Expanding rural banks/cooperatives and strengthening SHG-bank linkage directly increase poor households’ share in cheap formal credit.

q: What practical advantages do modern paper currency and bank deposits have over commodity money (grain/cattle) or metallic coins?
o: They are portable, standardised, divisible, backed by government authority, and bank deposits allow safe cashless settlement via cheques or transfers
They can be eaten as food during droughts
They cannot be stored in banks
They require barter coincidence
e: Modern currency and demand deposits are portable, divisible, legally accepted nationwide, and enable safe cashless payments.

q: Why could Arun hold his potato crop in cold storage to wait for higher prices while Shyamal had to sell his crop immediately to the trader?
o: Arun had a cheap 8.5% bank loan repayable over 3 years allowing him to hold stock for better prices, whereas Shyamal’s trader-lender forced an immediate sale condition at harvest
Shyamal refused higher crop prices
Cold storage was illegal for 1.5-acre plots
Banks banned Arun from selling potatoes
e: Traders often lend on harsh repayment conditions binding small farmers to sell produce to them right at harvest when prices are low, unlike flexible bank credit.

q: If RBI stopped monitoring whom commercial banks lend to, what would be the most likely negative consequence?
o: Banks would lend almost exclusively to profit-making big businesses and traders, neglecting small cultivators, small-scale industries, and small borrowers
Banks would voluntarily lend 100% at 0% interest to labourers
Informal moneylenders would disappear
Cheques would become illegal
e: RBI supervision ensures banks do not focus solely on profit-making big businesses but also extend formal credit to small farmers and small-scale borrowers.

q: Based on Swapna’s case in NCERT, what makes agricultural credit particularly risky for small farmers?
o: Farming depends on uncertain weather and pest risks while requiring upfront input credit; if crops fail, income vanishes and the farmer must borrow again or sell land
Because harvests occur weekly
Because moneylenders always waive loans after crop failure
Because inputs cost zero rupees
e: Crop failure destroys expected harvest income needed to repay seasonal credit, trapping small farmers like Swapna into fresh high-interest borrowing and asset sales.

q: How does borrowing through a Self-Help Group (SHG) differ fundamentally from borrowing from a village moneylender?
o: SHGs charge reasonable low interest, members collectively decide loan terms, and link women to formal bank credit without collateral; moneylenders charge exorbitant rates risking debt traps
SHGs charge 60% annual interest while moneylenders charge 2%
SHGs exclude rural women
Moneylenders are supervised by RBI
e: SHGs free poor borrowers from exploitative moneylenders by providing timely, low-interest loans decided democratically by members and backed by bank linkages.

q: A shopkeeper deposits Rs 50,000 from daily sales into a bank demand deposit account. What dual benefit does this create for the shopkeeper and the economy?
o: The shopkeeper gets safety, earns interest, and can withdraw or issue cheques anytime, while the bank channels the majority (~85%) of funds into productive loans across the economy
The cash remains frozen for 10 years
The bank cancels the shopkeeper’s ownership
Interest rates fall to zero
e: Bank deposits safely earn interest and stay liquid for the depositor while mobilising savings into productive economic credit.

q: Identify the correct historical sequence in the evolution of money as outlined in NCERT:
o: Barter/Commodity objects (grains, cattle) -> Metallic coins (gold, silver, copper) -> Modern paper currency, coins & bank demand deposits/cheques
Paper notes -> Barter -> Gold coins
Cheques -> Cattle -> Copper coins
Metallic coins -> Barter -> Digital cheques
e: Evolution progressed from early grains and cattle to metallic coins (gold, silver, copper) and finally to modern government-authorised currency and bank deposits.

q: Are paper notes and coins alone money in a modern economy, or do bank deposits also count? Choose the accurate explanation:
o: Both—modern forms of money closely link currency (paper notes and coins) and demand deposits with banks (which settle payments via cheques without cash)
Only paper notes count as money
Only gold bullion is legal tender
Bank deposits cannot be used for payments
e: Modern money comprises both currency (notes/coins) and demand deposits in banks, closely linking banking to everyday exchange.

q: A daily-wage woman needs Rs 30,000 to repair her home or buy a sewing machine. What barrier does she face at a formal bank, and how does an SHG solve it?
o: The bank demands collateral and formal income documents she lacks; through an SHG with 1–2 years of regular savings, the bank sanctions a loan in the group’s name without individual collateral
The bank immediately lends at 200% interest
The SHG confiscates her house
Banks are forbidden from lending to women
e: SHGs bridge the collateral gap: once the group shows 1–2 years of regular savings, banks gladly sanction collateral-free loans in the group’s name.

q: Rich households mostly borrow formally for productive investment or housing, whereas poor households often borrow informally for medical emergencies or daily needs. What is the difference in outcome?
o: Productive low-interest borrowing expands assets and income, whereas high-interest informal borrowing for consumption/emergencies drains borrower earnings into interest
High-interest consumption loans double poor households’ assets
Moneylenders never charge interest on medical loans
Outcomes are identical
e: Affordable credit used productively boosts income, while high-interest informal credit for non-income-generating needs increases debt-trap vulnerability.

q: In what situation can the cost of borrowing from an informal source exceed the borrower’s entire extra earnings?
o: When informal lenders charge exorbitant rates like 3–5% per month (36–60% per annum), causing debt repayment to consume all earnings and even exceed total income
When a bank charges 8% per annum
When a cooperative lends for irrigation
When a relative lends interest-free
e: Higher cost of borrowing means a larger share of earnings is spent repaying loans; sometimes the amount to be repaid exceeds the borrower’s total income, triggering a debt trap.

q: What crucial economic principle did the success of Prof. Muhammad Yunus’s Grameen Bank of Bangladesh establish?
o: If credit can be made available to the poor (especially poor women) on terms and conditions that are appropriate and reasonable, these millions of small people with their millions of small pursuits can add up to create the biggest development wonder
That poor borrowers always default on loans
That only wealthy corporations deserve formal credit
That microcredit cannot work in villages
e: Reaching over 9 million members across 81,600 villages by 2018, Grameen Bank proved poor women are reliable borrowers capable of running diverse income-generating enterprises.

q:
Match the Sonpur borrowers in NCERT with their actual lender and annual/monthly interest rate:
A. Shyamal (1.5 acres)
B. Arun (7 acres)
C. Rama (Landless labourer)

q: Why do some small rural farmers still approach moneylenders even where formal bank branches exist nearby?
o: (1) Difficulty meeting collateral and documentation requirements at banks, and (2) urgent need for timely/emergency credit without lengthy formalities (or previous unpaid dues)
(1) Moneylenders charging lower rates than banks (2% p.a.), and (2) banks banning rural accounts
(1) Banks operating only at midnight
(1) RBI prohibiting agricultural credit
e: Complex bank documentation, collateral demands, and delays/urgent cash needs still push vulnerable farmers toward accessible yet costly moneylenders.

q: Synthesising the stories of Shyamal (1.5 acres), Arun (7 acres), and Rama (landless labourer) in Sonpur village, what structural pattern is revealed?
o: Access and cost of credit are inversely skewed by asset ownership: richer landowners get cheap 8.5% formal bank loans, while small farmers and landless workers pay 36–60% informal interest
Landless labourers get the cheapest formal loans
Everyone in villages pays an identical 8.5%
Banks refuse 7-acre farmers
e: Arun (7 acres) pays 8.5% to a bank, Shyamal (1.5 acres) pays 36% to a trader, and landless Rama pays 60% to her employer—showing the poorest pay the highest cost for credit.

q: Modern cashless payments (whether via cheques or bank transfers) fundamentally depend on what underlying financial asset?
o: Demand deposits held in bank accounts within the government-authorised currency and RBI-regulated banking system
Gold ornaments stored at home
Grain sacks exchanged directly
Moneylenders’ verbal promises
e: All cashless cheque or bank-account settlements ultimately transfer funds between demand deposit accounts regulated under the Rupee system.

q: Identify the INCORRECT statement regarding the role of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI):
o: RBI issues currency notes on behalf of the Central Government
RBI monitors that commercial banks actually maintain the minimum cash balance (~15%)
RBI requires banks to submit periodic reports on lending volume, borrowers, and interest rates
RBI directly fixes interest rates and daily audits every village moneylender’s register
e: Moneylenders are in the informal sector, where NCERT explicitly states no organisation supervises their credit activities.

q:
Consider these statements about the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh:
1. It started in the 1970s as a small project under Prof. Muhammad Yunus.
2. By 2018, it had over 9 million members spread across about 81,600 villages.
3. Almost all its borrowers are women from the poorest sections of society.
Which statements are correct?
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
All 1, 2 and 3
e: All three facts are accurately stated in the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh case box in NCERT.

q: Which pair represents the safest and most affordable institutional credit channels for small rural borrowers seeking Rs 40,000 for farming or self-employment?
o: A farmers’ cooperative society (like Krishak Cooperative) OR a bank-linked Self-Help Group (SHG)
A village landlord and moneylending crop trader
An unregulated urban informal lender
Barter exchange only
e: Both cooperative societies and bank-linked SHGs deliver low-interest formal credit without exploitative recovery conditions.

q: A student asks: "Why do banks pay interest on money they hold for depositors while charging higher interest to borrowers?" What is the exact economic explanation?
o: Deposit interest encourages people to save surplus money with banks; lending those funds at a higher interest rate earns the interest spread that funds bank operations and profits
Banks charge equal rates so their revenue stays zero
Banks deduct 20% from savings deposits
Interest rates are set randomly
e: Deposit interest mobilises savings into banks, and the higher lending rate generates the spread covering operations, risk, and bank income.

q: Which economic mechanism directly connects "Sectors of the Indian Economy" (unorganised sector/small farmers) with "Money and Credit"?
o: The ~80% marginal rural farmers and urban small workshops in the unorganised sector suffer without cheap formal credit; rural banks, cooperatives, and SHGs solve this to boost jobs and output
Credit has zero impact on agriculture or industry
Organised sector salaries are paid in wheat bags
GDP excludes banking completely
e: Expanding cheap formal credit to small farmers and small-scale workshops directly strengthens rural employment and incomes across sectors.

q: If RBI raised the minimum cash balance requirement for commercial banks from 15% to 30%, what would be its immediate impact on banks’ lending capacity?
o: Out of every Rs 100 deposited, banks can lend less (Rs 70 instead of Rs 85), reducing overall credit supply
Banks could lend double the deposits
It leaves lending capacity unchanged
Cheques become illegal immediately
e: Holding a higher cash reserve leaves a smaller share of total deposits available for banks to advance as loans.

q: Which statement provides an INCORRECT analysis of the "Two different credit situations" in NCERT?
o: In Salim’s case, credit helped meet working capital and raised earnings
In Swapna’s case, crop failure made repayment impossible and pushed her into a debt trap
Whether credit helps or harms depends on situational risks and support in case of loss
Swapna’s case proves farmers must never borrow from formal banks either
e: Swapna borrowed from an expensive moneylender and suffered crop failure; the lesson is improving affordable credit and risk support, not rejecting formal credit.

q: RBI monitoring to ensure banks lend not only to big profitable businesses but also to small cultivators and small borrowers addresses which major market gap?
o: The tendency of profit-driven banks to favour large commercial borrowers with easy collateral while neglecting small rural producers
Excess cash idle inside farmer accounts
Shortage of paper for cheques
Over-lending to landless labourers
e: Without regulatory oversight, profit-focused banks naturally prefer big, collateral-backed businesses, leaving small farmers and small enterprises underserved.

q: Comparing Megha’s housing loan (Rs 5 lakh, 12% p.a., 10 years) and Arun’s crop loan (8.5% p.a., 3 years), what common feature do both illustrate?
o: Both are formal sector bank loans featuring reasonable annual interest rates, clear repayment schedules, and transparent collateral/documentation terms
Both are 60% informal loans
Neither required any documentation
Both resulted in debt traps
e: Both Megha and Arun used formal bank credit characterised by reasonable annual interest rates and transparent repayment/collateral agreements.

q: Farmer X has 2 acres with incomplete title deeds, while Worker Y is completely landless. Why are Cooperatives and SHGs especially helpful compared to standard commercial bank loans?
o: Both pool collective deposits or regular savings discipline to overcome individual collateral/title barriers and deliver affordable formal credit
Both lend crores without any savings record
Both charge 5% per month interest
Both exclude rural households
e: Pooled cooperative deposits and regular SHG savings overcome individual collateral/document gaps to provide affordable credit.

q: As cheque and digital bank-account payments expand rapidly in India, how does the role of "Demand Deposits" evolve?
o: The importance of demand deposits increases further because cashless cheques and bank transfers directly draw upon demand deposit balances
Demand deposits become obsolete
Commercial banks shut down
Rupee legal tender ceases
e: Cashless payments settle directly between bank accounts, reinforcing the central role of demand deposits as modern money.

q: What explains the paradox: "Formal credit is cheap yet hard for the poor to get, while informal credit is costly yet readily available"?
o: Banks require documentation and collateral and are absent in many villages, whereas informal moneylenders know borrowers personally and lend immediately without collateral—charging exorbitant rates later
Banks charge 60% interest to poor people
Rural households dislike low interest rates
Moneylenders represent RBI
e: Bridging this gap requires expanding rural bank branches, simplifying documentation, and scaling up SHG-bank linkage.

q: Which traditional banking prejudice did the Grameen Bank of Bangladesh (over 9 million members across 81,600 villages, mostly poor women) decisively disprove?
o: The notion that asset-less ultra-poor people—especially rural women—are not creditworthy and will fail to repay loans without collateral
The rule that banks hold ~15% cash
The principle that money acts as a medium of exchange
The practice of using cheques
e: Grameen Bank and India’s SHGs proved that poor women are exceptionally reliable borrowers who successfully run small income-generating activities.

q: Can two borrowers taking loans at the same interest rate experience completely opposite outcomes (profit vs debt trap)?
o: Yes, because outcomes depend heavily on the level of risk in the activity (e.g., guaranteed festival footwear order vs weather/pest-vulnerable crop) and support against losses
No, equal interest rates guarantee identical profits
No, loans never cause losses
Yes, only if borrowed in foreign currency
e: Situational risk (such as harvest failure vs confirmed industrial order) and loss support determine whether credit helps or harms.

q: Which complete set of four components must any borrower carefully evaluate as "Terms of Credit" before signing a loan agreement?
o: Interest rate, Collateral, Documentation requirement, and Mode of repayment
Bank building size, manager’s name, city population, and ATM colour
Only currency weight and serial numbers
Only bank holidays and cheque colour
e: Interest rate, collateral, documentation, and mode of repayment together define the Terms of Credit.

q: If poor households obtain 85% of their loans from expensive informal sources, what is the single biggest socio-economic consequence?
o: Poor families’ earnings are drained by high interest, preventing productive investment in farms or micro-enterprises and perpetuating poverty across generations
Banks earn too little money from big corporations
RBI halts currency issuance
Urbanisation slows to zero
e: High informal borrowing costs trap poor families out of productive investment, reinforcing NCERT’s conclusion that cheap formal credit is vital for development.

q: Expanding rural cooperative/bank branches and assuring SHG linkage after 12 months of saving directly reduces the gap in—
o: The stark formal-credit gap between rich households (90% formal) and poor households (only 15% formal)
Solely the printing cost of paper cheques
International crude oil reserves
Tariffs on imported toys
e: Expanding rural banks, cooperatives, and SHG linkages directly narrows the massive formal-credit gap between rich and poor households.

q: Which option accurately represents the basic arithmetic of commercial bank intermediation described in NCERT?
o: Deposits = Rs 100 -> Cash reserve held ≈ Rs 15 -> Funds extended as loans ≈ Rs 85; with Lending interest rate > Deposit interest rate
Deposits = Rs 100 -> Cash reserve = Rs 100 -> Loans = Rs 0
Deposits = Rs 100 -> Cash reserve = Rs 85 -> Loans = Rs 15; 0% spread
Deposits = Rs 100 -> Transferred entirely to moneylenders
e: Banks retain ~15% cash reserve, lend ~85% of deposits, and earn income from the positive spread between lending and deposit interest rates.

q: What could undermine public trust in modern banking and currency systems?
o: Allowing private entities to issue currency arbitrarily or removing RBI supervision over banks’ cash reserves and lending practices
Settling business deals using bank cheques
Encouraging regular savings in SHGs
Providing 8.5% crop loans to farmers
e: RBI’s sole authority over currency issuance and active supervision of commercial banks preserve public confidence in money and banking.

q: Students often compare a moneylender’s "5% rate" with a bank’s "10% rate". What crucial detail must always be checked to avoid an error?
o: The compounding period (per month vs per annum): 5% per month equals 60% per annum, whereas a bank’s 10% is per annum!
Both are always charged per day
Bank interest is monthly while moneylender interest is per decade
5% per month equals 5% per year
e: Informal moneylenders quote rates per month (3–5% per month = 36–60% per annum), whereas banks quote annual rates (8.5–12% per annum).

q: What is the overarching economic message of the chapter "Money and Credit"?
o: Money simplifies exchange, and expanding cheap, supervised formal credit (via banks, cooperatives, and SHGs) while guarding against high-risk informal debt traps is vital for equitable development
Barter is more efficient than modern currency
Poor villagers thrive best under unregulated moneylenders
Formal banking should serve only wealthy urban households
e: Government-authorised money plus widespread, affordable formal credit (banks, cooperatives, and SHGs) free the poor from exploitative debt traps and fuel inclusive growth.
